In [[number theory]], a [[Congruence relation|congruence]] is an [[equivalence relation]] on the [[integer]]s.  The following sections list important or interesting prime-related congruences.

==Table of congruences characterizing special primes==

{| class="wikitable" 
|- style="text-align:center;"
! Congruence !! Explanation !! Known examples
|-
| <math>2^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{p}</math> || special case of [[Fermat's little theorem]], satisfied by all odd [[prime number]]s ||
|-
| <math>2^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{p^2}</math> || solutions are called [[Wieferich prime]]s || 1093, 3511 ({{OEIS2C|A001220}})
|-
| <math>F_{n - \left(\frac{{n}}{{5}}\right)} \equiv 0 \pmod{n}</math> || satisfied by all [[prime numbers]] ||
|-
| <math>F_{p - \left(\frac{{p}}{{5}}\right)} \equiv 0 \pmod{p^2}</math> || solutions are called [[Wall–Sun–Sun prime]]s || no examples known
|-
| <math>{2n-1 \choose n-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{n^3}</math> || by [[Wolstenholme's theorem]] satisfied by all [[prime number]]s greater than 3 ||
|-
| <math>{2p-1 \choose p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{p^4},</math> || solutions are called [[Wolstenholme prime]]s || 16843, 2124679 ({{OEIS2C|A088164}})
|-
| <math>(n-1)!\ \equiv\ -1 \pmod n</math> || by [[Wilson's theorem]] a natural number ''n'' is prime [[if and only if]] it satisfies this congruence ||
|-
| <math>(p-1)!\ \equiv\ -1 \pmod{p^2}</math> || solutions are called [[Wilson prime]]s || 5, 13, 563 ({{OEIS2C|A007540}})
|-
| <math>4[(p-1)!+1]\ \equiv\ -p \pmod{p(p+2)}</math> || solutions are the [[twin primes]] ||
|}

==Other prime-related congruences==

There are other prime-related congruences that provide necessary and sufficient conditions on the primality of certain subsequences of the natural numbers. 
Many of these alternate statements characterizing primality are related to [[Wilson's theorem]], or are restatements of this classical result given in terms of other 
special variants of [[Double factorial#Generalizations|generalized factorial functions]]. For instance, new variants of [[Wilson's theorem]] stated in terms of the 
[[hyperfactorials]], [[subfactorials]], and [[superfactorials]] are given in.<ref>{{cite journal|last1 = Aebi | first1 = Christian | last2 = Cairns |first2 = Grant |title=Generalizations of Wilson's Theorem for Double-, Hyper-, Sub- and Superfactorials|journal=The American Mathematical Monthly|date=May 2015|volume=122|issue=5|pages=433–443|jstor=10.4169/amer.math.monthly.122.5.433|doi=10.4169/amer.math.monthly.122.5.433| s2cid = 207521192 }}</ref>

===Variants of Wilson's theorem===

For integers <math>k \geq 1</math>, we have the following form of Wilson's theorem: 
:<math>(k-1)! (p-k)! \equiv (-1)^k \pmod{p} \iff p \text{ prime. } </math> 
If <math>p</math> is odd, we have that 
:<math>\left(\frac{p-1}{2}\right)!^2 \equiv (-1)^{(p+1)/2} \pmod{p} \iff p \text{ an odd prime. } </math>

===Clement's theorem concerning the twin primes===

Clement's congruence-based theorem characterizes the [[twin primes]] pairs of the form <math>(p, p+2)</math> through the following conditions: 
:<math> 4[(p-1)!+1] \equiv -p \pmod{p(p+2)} \iff p,p+2 \text{ are both prime. } </math> 
P. A. Clement's original 1949 paper <ref>{{cite journal|last1=Clement|first1=P. A.|title=Congruences for sets of primes|journal=Amer. Math. Monthly|date=1949|volume=56|issue=1|pages=23–25|doi=10.2307/2305816|jstor=2305816}}</ref> provides a 
proof of this interesting elementary number theoretic criteria for twin primality based on Wilson's theorem. 
Another characterization given in Lin and Zhipeng's article provides that 
:<math> 2 \left(\frac{p-1}{2}\right)!^2 + (-1)^{\frac{p-1}{2}} (5p+2) \equiv 0 \iff  p,p+2 \text{ are both prime. } </math>

===Characterizations of prime tuples and clusters===

The prime pairs of the form <math>(p, p+2k)</math> for some <math>k \geq 1</math> include the special cases of the [[cousin primes]] (when <math>k=2</math>) and the [[sexy primes]]  (when <math>k=3</math>). We have elementary congruence-based characterizations of the primality of such pairs, proved for instance in the article.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=C. Lin and L. Zhipeng|title=On Wilson's theorem and Polignac conjecture|journal=Math. Medley|date=2005|volume=6|arxiv=math/0408018|bibcode=2004math......8018C}}</ref> Examples of congruences characterizing these prime pairs include 
:<math>2k (2k)![(p-1)!+1] \equiv [1-(2k)!]p \pmod{p(p+2k)} \iff p,p+2k \text{ are both prime, }</math> 
and the alternate characterization when <math>p</math> is odd such that <math>p \not{\mid} (2k-1)!!^2</math> given by 
:<math>2k(2k-1)!!^2 \left(\frac{p-1}{2}\right)!^2 + (-1)^{\frac{p-1}{2}}\left[(2k-1)!!^2(p+2k)-(-4)^k \cdot p\right] \equiv 0 \iff p,p+2k \text{ are both prime. } </math> 
Still other congruence-based characterizations of the primality of triples, and more general [[Prime k-tuple|prime clusters]] (or [[Prime k-tuple|prime tuples]]) exist and are typically proved starting from Wilson's theorem.<ref>See, for example, Section 3.3 in {{cite journal
 | last = Schmidt | first = Maxie D.
 | arxiv = 1701.04741
 | journal = Integers
 | mr = 3862591
 | article-number=A78
 | title = New congruences and finite difference equations for generalized factorial functions
 | volume = 18
 | year = 2018}}</ref>).
